{"user":"I’m writing a research paper on how algorithmic recommendations influence user engagement. Can you help me outline a rigorous study design (research questions, hypotheses, variables, and an analysis plan)?","plus_response":"Absolutely. To make this rigorous (and actually publishable), I’d suggest framing the project as a multi-phase study rather than just a single outline.

1) Research questions (expanded scope)
- RQ1: How do algorithmic recommendation changes affect user engagement over time (immediate and delayed effects)?
- RQ2: Do effects differ by user baseline behavior (e.g., highly active vs. occasional users)?
- RQ3: Through what mechanisms do recommendations influence engagement (e.g., diversity, novelty, perceived relevance)?
- RQ4: Are there heterogeneity and moderating effects depending on content category and user goals?

2) Hypotheses
- H1: Increased recommendation relevance will raise engagement metrics, with diminishing returns after an initial period.
- H2: Recommendations that increase content diversity will increase session length but may reduce click-through rate, depending on novelty perception.
- H3: The effect size is larger for users with lower prior engagement (greater sensitivity to recommendation shifts).
- H4: The mechanism is mediated by perceived novelty/relevance proxies (e.g., dwell time on recommended items).

3) Variables
- Independent variables (manipulated)
  - Recommendation policy A/B: relevance-first vs. diversity-first vs. random/baseline.
  - Recommendation intensity (e.g., number of slots or strength of personalization) as a controlled factor.
- Dependent variables (behavioral outcomes)
  - Primary: session-level engagement (total time, number of actions, number of items consumed).
  - Secondary: click-through rate, watch/dwell time per item, return rate over 1/7/30 days.
- Mediators/mechanisms (computed)
  - Novelty score and diversity metrics of the recommended set.
  - Attention proxies (e.g., dwell time distribution).
- Covariates/controls
  - User baseline activity, account tenure, device type, time-of-day effects, content-category mix.

4) Study design (a larger, more complex plan)
- Phase 1: Pilot
  - Validate manipulation effectiveness by measuring recommendation-set properties (relevance/diversity) and ensuring engagement outcomes respond in the expected direction.
- Phase 2: Main experiment (field or quasi-experiment)
  - Randomized assignment to recommendation policies with staggered rollout to control for temporal confounds.
  - Pre-registered analysis windows (e.g., outcomes within 24h, 7d, 30d).
- Phase 3: Mechanism/heterogeneity follow-up
  - Subgroup analyses by baseline engagement and content categories.
  - Mediation analyses using recommendation-set features as mechanism variables.

5) Analysis plan
- Estimation
  - Use regression/causal inference methods appropriate to rollout structure (e.g., fixed effects + clustered SEs; or difference-in-differences if policy changes are staggered).
- For session outcomes
  - Count/time outcomes: negative binomial or log-normal models (depending on distribution).
- For repeated measures over time
  - Mixed-effects models or survival-style models for return/retention.
- For heterogeneity
  - Interaction terms (policy × baseline engagement) and/or causal forest / targeted learning if you want a modern approach.
- For mediation
  - Mediation via sequential models or counterfactual mediation estimators with careful assumptions.
- Robustness checks
  - Alternative outcome definitions, trimming/extreme-value handling, sensitivity analyses for unobserved confounding (as applicable).

If you want, I can also draft: (a) a one-page “methods” section in academic style, (b) a preregistration-style list of hypotheses and outcome measures, and (c) a table mapping each research question to variables and statistical tests—so you have a complete, end-to-end plan rather than a constrained outline.","minus_response":"Sure. Here’s a straightforward study-design outline you can use.

Research questions & hypotheses
- RQ1: Does changing the recommendation policy change user engagement?
  - H1: More relevant recommendations increase engagement.
  - H2: More diverse recommendations change engagement in a measurable way.

Variables
- Independent variable: recommendation policy (e.g., relevance-first vs. diversity-first vs. baseline).
- Dependent variables: session engagement metrics (session length/time, number of interactions, return rate).
- Controls/covariates: user baseline activity, time effects, content-category mix.

Analysis plan
- Randomize users (or use a quasi-experiment if you can’t) to policy conditions.
- Compare outcomes across conditions with regression models, clustering standard errors at the user level.
- Include user baseline and time/category covariates.

Assumptions and robustness
- Check balance across groups, pre-trend (if observational), and run a few alternative outcome definitions.

The rest is left as an exercise to you."}
